upstreamForm.description: The API the gate calls. Saved to moat.yaml; on the gate, the change applies only with the next bundle.
upstreamForm.name: Name
upstreamForm.originHint: Only https:// and the host, no path. The gate’s policy must allow the host.
upstreamForm.timeoutHint: Empty means 10 seconds. With a unit, e.g. 5s, at most 60s.
upstreamForm.secretHint: Only the name, never the key itself. Then seal the key in the terminal for each gate: `moat secret seal <gate> <name>`.
upstreamForm.refused: Moat did not save the upstream: the marked fields hold values the gate would refuse.

form.description: Saved to moat.yaml. On the gate, the route applies only with the next bundle.
form.name: Name
form.nameHint: Lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, starting with a letter, e.g. newsletter.
form.pathHint: Starts with /, no / at the end. Matched exactly: /newsletter does not match /newsletter/abc.
form.maxBodySizeHint: Empty means 64 KiB. With a unit: B, KiB or MiB, at most 10 MiB.
form.originsHint: One address per line, e.g. https://www.example.ch. Empty means no other website may call the route in a browser.
form.windowHint: A window with a unit in whole seconds, e.g. 30s, 10m, 1h, at most 1d. The local policy’s limits always apply as well.
form.quotaHint: Counts all requests to this route together, whoever sends them. The day starts at midnight UTC, the month on the 1st. Once the quota is used up, the gate answers 429 with quota_exceeded until then.
form.budgetMaxOutput: Output tokens per request at most
form.budgetHint: Every request to the route must bound its cost: no stream, max_tokens (maxOutputTokens for Gemini) up to the value above, and no tools the provider runs itself (web search, code execution). The gate refuses others with 400 and request_unbounded. Before forwarding it books the request's most possible usage (its size in bytes plus max_tokens) and afterwards replaces it with the usage the answer reports; when the answer cannot be counted, the most possible usage stays booked. Set tokens, cost or both; amounts in the provider's currency, e.g. 20.00, prices as the provider lists them per million tokens. Once the budget is reached, the gate answers 429 with budget_exhausted until the day or month ends (UTC).
form.refused: Moat did not save the route: the marked fields hold values the gate would refuse.

help.title: Help
help.subtitle: Step by step from moat.yaml to a running gate

intro.title: How Moat works
intro.body: Moat keeps your API keys out of the browser. The gate runs on your hosting and forwards only the routes you approve. You write the configuration in moat.yaml, sign it with your key file and upload it to the gate. Moat Desktop shows you what is ready in your project folders.

noProject.question: “Projects” says “No project yet”.
noProject.answer: Click “Add project” and choose the folder that holds your moat.yaml. Moat Desktop remembers the folder; you add more projects the same way.

invalidConfig.question: moat.yaml contains errors. What now?
invalidConfig.answer: The project overview names every error with line and column. Fix the file in your editor and click “Reload”. Typical causes are missing quotes around paths and URLs, or a typo in an upstream name.

missingSecret.question: Under “Gates” a gate is missing a secret.
missingSecret.answer: An upstream needs a secret that is not sealed for this gate yet. Seal it with `moat secret seal <gate> <name>`; you type the value in the terminal, and it never lands in the project folder in plain text.

fingerprint.question: The fingerprint does not match the gate's.
fingerprint.answer: Then the gate file does not belong to your gate. Delete it, check the output of `php moat-gate.php status` on the server and add the gate again with `moat gate add`.

lockPending.question: I locked a gate, but it still forwards.
lockPending.answer: So far the lock is only in moat.yaml. It applies once the gate has accepted a bundle that carries it: sign a new bundle (“Sign bundle” or `moat build <gate>`), upload the file and run `php moat-gate.php accept` on the server. `php moat-gate.php status` then shows `LOCKED`.

setup.title: Setup
setup.purpose: The setup wizard takes you through everything a gate needs on the first start. Moat saves your progress, you can continue at any time.
setup.where: Setup, at the bottom of the sidebar

steps.language: Under “Language”, choose how Moat speaks to you.
steps.key: Under “Signing key”, create your key file with “Create a new key”, or choose one you already have with “Choose an existing key file”. You type the passphrase only in Moat's own window.
steps.project: Under “First project”, create a project folder with “Create a new project”, or add an existing one with “Add an existing folder”.
steps.gate: Under “First gate”, install the gate with the command shown, enter the gate ID and box key and click “Check”. Compare the fingerprint with the gate's output and confirm with “It matches”.
steps.recipe: Under “First recipe”, choose a ready-made route and click “Apply”. Seal the secret with “Seal”, sign with “Sign bundle” and install the policy from “Show policy” and the bundle on the server. “Test” then sends a request through the gate.
steps.summary: The “Summary” shows what is set up, the trust mode and the hardening level. “Finish” opens your project.

tips.later: You skip optional steps with “Later”. The summary keeps showing them.
tips.again: “Setup” in the sidebar opens the wizard again at any time.

project.title: Projects
project.purpose: Each website is a project. Everything Moat knows about it lives in its project folder: the configuration, the gates, the sealed secrets and the signed bundles. No database, no server.

steps.cli: Create a folder and write a moat.yaml in it. A recipe from the `recipes` folder is a good start.
steps.folder: The Moat CLI adds the subfolders: `gates` for the gates, `secrets` for sealed secrets, `bundles` for signed bundles.
steps.add: Under “Projects”, click “Add project” and choose the folder. The project opens right away.
steps.create: Or let Moat create the folder: “Setup” › “First project” › “Create a new project” writes a valid `moat.yaml` into it.
steps.check: Every project has the parts “Overview”, “Gates” and “Routes”. The overview shows whether moat.yaml is valid, how many routes, upstreams, secrets and gates there are, and which trust mode applies.

tips.git: The project folder works well with Git: secrets are only stored sealed, and key files do not belong in it.
tips.reload: When you change files in the folder, click “Reload”.
tips.remove: “Remove from list” only takes the entry away. The folder and its files stay as they are.

gate.title: Install a gate
gate.purpose: The gate runs on your hosting. It knows your secrets and forwards only the routes you approve. It has no management interface that could be reached from outside.

steps.upload: Upload the file moat-gate.php to your website's web space.
steps.install: On the server, run `php moat-gate.php install --signer=<public key>`. The gate creates a protected data folder and prints its gate ID, box key and fingerprints.
steps.add: Add the gate to your project folder with the `moat gate add` line the gate printed.
steps.addDesktop: In Moat Desktop you enter the gate under “Setup” › “First gate” and compare the fingerprint there before it is saved.
steps.compare: Compare the fingerprint the CLI prints group by group with the gate's.
steps.check: Under “Gates” you see every gate you added, with gate ID and fingerprint.

tips.mismatch: If a group differs, delete the gate file and add the gate again.
tips.php: The gate needs PHP 8.2 or newer with the extensions sodium, curl, json and hash.

hardening.title: Check the hosting
hardening.purpose: The hardening check shows how well your hosting protects the gate's keys and secrets, and what you can improve. It runs on the server, on the gate's command line, and sends nothing to Moat.
hardening.where: On the server, in the folder of moat-gate.php

steps.run: Run `php moat-gate.php check --url=https://<your-site>/<path>/moat-gate.php` with the public address of the gate file.
steps.outside: The gate then fetches its own data files over the internet, the way anyone could. If one of them comes back, it reports `data_reachable`.
steps.process: The check also reaches the gate itself. That way the web server records which user PHP runs as and whether open_basedir is set.
steps.level: At the end you see the hardening level: `H1, Basic` or `H1, Unsafe for secrets`. If something is missing for a safe verdict, it says `not determined`.
steps.fix: Below the level, every finding comes with a recommendation. Fix all `unsafe` ones before you bind secrets to this gate.
steps.desktop: In Moat Desktop, “Check from outside” under “Gates” checks whether the gate's files can be read from the internet. Enter the address of the gate file and the “Data folder”; Moat asks in a window of its own whether it may reach that address. If a file is readable, Moat shows “Unsafe for secrets”. If none is, Moat shows no level, because only the gate itself determines it.

tips.shared: If all websites on the server run as the same user (such as www-data) and open_basedir is not set, other websites could read the gate's files. Ask your hoster for a separate PHP user per website.
tips.again: Run the check again after every change to the hosting. It exits with code 1 when the gate is unsafe for secrets, and 3 when it cannot determine a level.
tips.stronger: Today the gate always keeps its data in the web space, so the check reports H1 at most. Higher levels come with later versions.

trust.title: Trust mode
trust.purpose: The trust mode decides who may approve changes to a gate. Moat Desktop always uses “Signed”: the gate accepts only bundles signed with your key file.
trust.where: Project › Overview › Trust mode and Gates

steps.keygen: Create a key file once with `moat keygen <file>.moatkey` and choose a good passphrase.
steps.keyDesktop: In Moat Desktop you create the key under “Setup” › “Signing key” with “Create a new key”.
steps.trust: Give the gate the public key when you install it (--signer). You can change it only on the gate itself, with `php moat-gate.php trust`.
steps.badge: Next to each gate you see its trust mode, with the sentence on what an attacker could do if Moat Cloud were hacked.

tips.passphrase: Keep the key file outside the project folder and back it up. Without it you cannot sign bundles any more.
tips.desktopOnly: Moat Desktop works without the Cloud: you approve every change yourself with your key file.

secrets.title: Upstreams and secrets
secrets.purpose: An upstream is the API the gate calls. Its key is a secret: it is sealed for one particular gate and can be opened only there.
secrets.where: Project › Gates › Secrets and Routes › Upstreams

steps.upstream: Under “Routes”, click “New upstream” next to the upstreams and fill in the address, the authentication and the secret’s name (e.g. `hubspot-token`), never its value. In moat.yaml: `secret: hubspot-token`.
steps.sealDesktop: Under “Gates”, click “Seal” in the “Secrets” list. A separate Moat Desktop window shows the gate and its fingerprint. Compare the fingerprint with the gate’s, then paste the value. Only encrypted text is stored.
steps.seal: In the CLI, seal the value with `moat secret seal <gate> <name>`. You type it in the terminal; only encrypted text is stored.
steps.check: Under “Gates”, the “Secrets” list shows for each gate which secrets are sealed and which are still missing.

tips.never: Moat never shows secrets, not even in Moat Desktop. It knows only their names and versions.
tips.rotate: A new key? Click “Seal again” (in the CLI: `--secret-version` with a higher number) and sign a new bundle.

routes.title: Routes and recipes
routes.purpose: A route is an address on your gate that forwards exactly one kind of request to an upstream. The gate refuses everything else.

steps.write: Under “Routes”, click “New route” and fill in method, path, upstream and target path. The three-dot menu at the end of each row has “Edit”, “Switch off” (disables the route without deleting it) and “Delete”. If you prefer your editor, write it into moat.yaml directly.
steps.recipe: For common cases there are recipes, for example the newsletter sign-up with HubSpot.
steps.origins: If another website calls the route in a browser, add it under “Allowed websites” (in moat.yaml: `origins`). Without an entry, browsers refuse other websites.
steps.body: So that only expected data reaches the API, list the fields your website sends under `body` in moat.yaml, with a type (`string`, `integer`, `boolean`, `object`, `array`) and bounds such as `required`, `maxLength`, `enum` or `format: email`. The gate removes every other field and refuses content that does not fit with 400 and `body_invalid`. The recipes bring their fields along. Under “Routes”, each route shows which fields are checked, or that its content is forwarded unchecked.
steps.bundle: A new or changed route applies on the gate only with the next bundle: `moat build <gate>`, upload it and accept it.
steps.check: Under “Routes” you see every route as the gate checks it: path, target, allowed websites, limits and maximum size.

tips.exact: Paths match exactly: `/newsletter` does not match `/newsletter/abc`.
tips.requireBody: When every route to an API that takes content lists its fields, `moat policy suggest` proposes `requireBody: true` for that host. The gate then accepts no bundle in which a route to that API takes content without fields, not even a signed one. A route without fields then needs `maxBodySize: '0B'`.
tips.quote: Put paths, URLs and durations in quotes, for example `'10m'`.

console.title: Test console
console.purpose: Before you sign, the test console shows what the gate would do with a request: which route it hits, whether the gate refuses it and why, and which call it would send to the API.

steps.route: Pick a route under “Start from a route”. Method, path, origin and Content-Type are filled in; you can change all of them.
steps.gate: Pick a gate under “Gate” so that its lock and its sealed secrets count. Without a gate, the console checks the configuration only.
steps.read: Under “How the gate would answer” you see the refusal with its code and reason, or the call to the API with method, address, headers and body.

tips.nothingSent: The console sends nothing: no gate, no API. Where the gate puts the secret, it shows `<SECRET>`.
tips.policy: The check uses the policy `moat policy suggest` proposes. The policy on your gate can differ, and the console does not see a local kill switch.
tips.counters: Rate limits, quotas and budgets appear as rules only. How much of them is used up, only the running gate knows.

limits.title: Limits
limits.purpose: Rate limits protect your API from scripts; quotas cap how much a route uses per day or month in total, and budgets how many tokens or how much money an AI API may cost. The gate counts by itself.

steps.route: Give a route a rate limit, for example 5 requests per 10 minutes per visitor.
steps.quota: Give a route a cap on all requests together with “Quota per day or month”, for example 1000 per day. Then nobody can burn your AI budget, not even from many addresses.
steps.budget: For an AI API such as OpenAI, Anthropic or Gemini, “Budget for an AI API” sets a limit in tokens, in cost or both, per day or month. Your website must then send each request with `max_tokens` up to “Output tokens per request at most” and without a stream, with only its own functions as tools (no web search or code execution at the provider, which is billed per call), otherwise the gate answers `request_unbounded`. It books the most possible usage before and what the answer used afterwards.
steps.policy: The gate's local policy sets limits that always apply, whatever a bundle says. It can also set a quota for the whole gate (`limits.quota`) and a token budget per upstream host (`budget` under `upstreams`) that no bundle can lift. `moat policy suggest` proposes a matching policy.
steps.answer: When a limit is reached, the gate answers 429 and says when to try again: `rate_limited` for a rate limit, `quota_exceeded` for a quota, `budget_exhausted` for a budget.

tips.proxy: If your website runs behind a proxy like Cloudflare, the gate sees only the proxy's address. Set the limits more generously then.

release.title: Approve and sign
release.purpose: A bundle is the signed configuration for exactly one gate. The gate accepts it only when the signature is valid and the version is higher than the last one.

steps.sign: Under “Gates”, click “Sign bundle” on the gate. A separate Moat Desktop window shows what changes since the last bundle. The first time, choose your key file (`.moatkey`), then enter the passphrase and confirm. The bundle is then saved under `bundles`.
steps.package: Under “Gates”, “Save as ZIP” or “Put into a folder” saves a deploy package: the latest signed bundle unchanged, the matching `policy.json` and instructions (`README.txt`) with the commands and the checksum. You choose where in Moat Desktop’s dialog. Moat packs only a bundle signed with your key file for this gate.
steps.sftp: Under “Gates”, “Upload via SFTP” puts the same package on your server as a new folder. You enter server, user, folder and password or SSH key in Moat Desktop’s window, never in the app page. The first time it shows the server’s host key: compare it with the one your hoster gives. Only then does Moat send user, password and files. If the server later shows another key, Moat stops. Moat replaces nothing on the server and runs no command there: you start `accept` yourself.
steps.git: If your hoster deploys from a Git repository, “Deliver via Git” under “Gates” puts the package as a new folder into your local working copy, commits only that folder and pushes it to the upstream of the checked-out branch. You choose the folder the first time; after that you confirm branch and remote every time. Moat uses your installed Git with your credentials but runs none of the repository’s hooks, and does not deliver into a repository whose own config starts programs. If the branch has commits that are not pushed yet, push them yourself first: Moat sends only the package. If the push fails, the commit stays and you push it yourself.
steps.import: Under “Gates”, “Import bundle” takes a signed bundle (`bundle-v<n>.json`) or a deploy package ZIP into the project, “Import package folder” the folder of a package. That way you work on several computers with the same key file, without the Cloud. Moat checks it as the gate does: the signature of your key file, the gate id, a higher version than the latest bundle and a valid configuration. Only the bundle is taken over, byte for byte. The `policy.json` in the package stays out: the policy belongs to the gate.
steps.build: In the CLI, build the bundle with `moat build <gate> --key <file>.moatkey`. It is then saved under `bundles`.
steps.deploy: Upload the bundle file to the server.
steps.accept: Activate it there with `php moat-gate.php accept <bundle>.json`. Under “Gates” you see the version built last.

tips.rollback: Back to an older configuration? Build it as a new, higher version.
tips.policy: If a bundle does not fit the local policy, the gate refuses it. You change the policy only on the gate itself.
tips.pull: No upload to the gate: if the local policy has a `pull` block with an HTTPS address, the gate fetches the bundle there itself, at most once per interval, and checks it as `accept` does. You then only upload the signed bundle to that address. `php moat-gate.php pull` fetches it at once, `php moat-gate.php status` shows the last attempt.
tips.keychain: If you like, Moat Desktop remembers the passphrase in your operating system’s keychain. Untick the box the next time you sign and it is deleted there. Without a real keychain, Moat Desktop does not offer this at all.
tips.sftpKeychain: Moat Desktop remembers the password or the key’s passphrase only in your operating system’s keychain, and only if you want it to. Without a real keychain it asks every time.

environments.title: Environments and locks
environments.purpose: Environments (such as dev, staging, production) group your gates. A whole environment or a single gate can be locked: a locked gate answers every request with an error and forwards nothing. The lock is signed into the bundle.

steps.define: In the “Overview”, under “Environments”, create an environment: type its name, then “Add environment”. Under “Gates”, choose each gate’s “Environment”. In the CLI: `moat env add staging` and `moat gate assign <gate> staging`.
steps.lock: Lock the whole environment with “Lock” on the “Environments” card, or a single gate with “Lock gate” under “Gates”. In the CLI: `moat env disable staging` or `moat gate disable <gate>`.
steps.build: Sign a new bundle for each gate concerned (with “Sign bundle” or `moat build <gate>`) and accept it on the gate with `php moat-gate.php accept`. Only then does the lock apply.
steps.check: In the “Overview”, the “Environments” card shows every environment with its gates; under “Gates”, every locked gate carries the “Locked” badge.

tips.unlock: Unlocking works the same way: “Unlock” or “Unlock gate” (in the CLI `moat env enable staging` or `moat gate enable <gate>`), then a new bundle.
tips.one: A gate belongs to at most one environment. While an environment is locked, unlocking a single gate in it changes nothing.
tips.answer: Visitors get status 503 with the code `gate_disabled` from a locked gate, even for paths that do not exist.
tips.saved: Every change goes into moat.yaml right away; comments and order stay as they are. If someone changed the file differently in the meantime, Moat saves nothing and reloads the project.

killSwitch.title: Kill switch
killSwitch.purpose: The kill switch turns a gate or a single route off at once, right on the server. It needs neither Moat Cloud nor a new bundle, and it works even when a bundle with a lock never arrives.
killSwitch.where: On the server, in the folder of moat-gate.php

steps.route: Turn a route off with `php moat-gate.php kill --route=<name>`, using the route's name from moat.yaml. From the next request on it answers 503 `route_disabled`; the other routes keep working.
steps.gate: Turn the whole gate off with `php moat-gate.php kill`. It then answers every request with 503 `gate_disabled` and forwards nothing.
steps.ftp: Without a command line, upload an empty file `kill.php` over FTP into the gate's data folder (the `moat-data-…` folder next to moat-gate.php). That turns the whole gate off.
steps.revive: Turn things on again with `php moat-gate.php revive --route=<name>` for one route or `php moat-gate.php revive` for everything. Without a command line, delete `kill.php` again.

tips.status: `php moat-gate.php status` shows what the kill switch currently turns off.
tips.closed: If `kill.php` holds something the gate does not understand, it turns the whole gate off rather than guess.
tips.age: Set `maxConfigAgeSeconds` in the local policy and `status` warns when the active bundle is older. That way you notice when a lock from the project never arrives.

privacy.title: Desktop and privacy
privacy.purpose: Moat Desktop works only on your computer. It needs no server and no account.

steps.local: Moat Desktop reads your project folder, writes changes only to its moat.yaml and sends nothing to the internet.
steps.ciphertext: Secrets are in the project folder only sealed. Only the gate they are sealed for can open them.
steps.noAdmin: The gate has no management that can be reached over the internet. It changes only through signed bundles and commands on the server.

tips.folder: You can back up the project folder like other files, for example with Git.

console.subtitle: Check a request before you sign: what would the gate do with this configuration? Nothing is sent.
console.unusable: The moat.yaml is not valid. The overview shows what is missing.
console.nothingSent: Only Moat calculates: no gate, no API, no secret.

notices.config_missing: The project folder has no moat.yaml.
notices.config_invalid: The moat.yaml is not valid. The overview shows what is missing.
notices.gate_unknown: The project no longer knows this gate. Reload the project.
notices.body_too_long: The body is too long. The console checks bodies up to 32 KiB.
notices.failed: The check did not work. Try again.

console.notAccepted: The gate would not accept this bundle at all ({{code}}): the configuration goes beyond the suggested policy.

errors.not_found: No route has exactly this path.
errors.method_not_allowed: The path exists, but not with this method.
errors.path_invalid: The path is invalid, for example because of “..” or encoded slashes.
errors.body_invalid: The content does not fit the route's fields: not a JSON object, a required field is missing, or a value has the wrong type or is out of bounds.
errors.request_unbounded: The route has a budget: the request must bound its cost (no stream, one answer, an output cap up to maxOutputTokens).
errors.body_too_large: The body is larger than the route or the policy allows.
errors.unsupported_media_type: This Content-Type is not allowed for the route.
errors.origin_forbidden: This website (origin) may not call the route.
errors.preflight_rejected: The browser would get no permission for this request (CORS).
errors.gate_disabled: The gate is locked and answers every request like this.
errors.gate_not_configured: The route names an upstream that does not exist.
errors.secret_unavailable: This upstream's secret is not sealed for the chosen gate.

console.preflight: The gate answers the preflight itself. The browser may then send the request.
console.forwarded: Through the route {{route}}, the gate would forward the request like this:
console.secret: The gate replaces {{placeholder}} with the sealed secret “{{secret}}”. The console does not know its value.

counters.perIp: at most {{requests}} requests per visitor in {{seconds}} s (suggested policy)
counters.total: at most {{requests}} requests in total in {{seconds}} s (suggested policy)

console.estimate: The budget is charged up front with {{input}} bytes of input and {{output}} tokens of output.
console.gateOnly: How far these counters are and what the API answers, only the running gate knows.
console.headersTitle: Headers from the gate to the browser
console.policyNote: Checked against the policy `moat policy suggest` proposes for this project. The policy on your gate can differ, and the console does not see a local kill switch.
